source: Qian et al. (2024) Scaling LLM-based Multi-Agent Collaboration (MacNet)
finding: Agents arranged in graphs (chain, star, tree, mesh, layer, random). Irregular random graphs did best on average. Quality rises with agent count in a logistic (S-shaped) curve.
numbers: Node count 2^0 to 2^6 in the fit (up to over a thousand agents in a mesh). Mean quality over MMLU, HumanEval, SRDD, CommonGen: CoT 0.5757, AgentVerse 0.5805, MacNet-Random 0.6522, Mesh 0.6316, Chain 0.6078. About 2^4 nodes judged a reasonable choice.
limits: Quality is a mixed average over four unlike benchmarks; per-task ranking varies a lot (MMLU: Random 0.6877 vs Layer 0.2780). Mostly one model family; not a human-team test.
agent_relevance: Team size gives S-shaped, not unlimited, gains. Do not assume more agents help past a small number.

source: Qian et al. (2024) Scaling LLM-based Multi-Agent Collaboration (MacNet) - topology detail
finding: No topology wins on every task. Chain was best on MMLU-like and SRDD; star and tree on CommonGen; HumanEval favoured AgentVerse.
numbers: HumanEval: AgentVerse 0.7256 vs MacNet-Chain 0.3720. CommonGen: Tree 0.7718, Star 0.7382, Chain 0.5903.
limits: Single-run table with one model; no significance tests.
agent_relevance: Team structure should match the task, not be fixed.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: 260 configurations: one single agent vs four team architectures (independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid) on six agentic benchmarks and three LLM families. Architecture-task fit, not agent count, decides the result.
numbers: Change vs single agent from +80.8% (decomposable finance, centralized) to -70.0% (sequential planning, independent). Cross-validated R2 = 0.373 (0.413 with a capability metric). Picks best architecture for 87% of held-out configs.
limits: R2 is modest; six fixed benchmarks; fitted model is correlational.
agent_relevance: Teams help only on decomposable work. Default to one thread for sequential reasoning.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems - error amplification
finding: Teams spread errors differently by structure. Independent agents with no cross-check amplify errors most; a central checker contains them.
numbers: Trace-level error amplification: single agent 1.0, centralized 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralized 7.8, independent 17.2.
limits: Measured from execution-trace token analysis, not ground-truth error rates.
agent_relevance: A verification bottleneck matters more than headcount. Supports G3 and G5.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems - capability ceiling
finding: Once a single agent already scores above about 45%, extra agents give negative returns. Tool-heavy tasks (16 tools) also lose from coordination cost.
numbers: Capability ceiling beta = -0.236 (p = 0.004); tool-coordination trade-off beta = -0.096 (p = 0.002). Planning: -39% to -70% for all multi-agent variants; Workbench -11% to -2%; non-agentic HumanEval 89% with five voters.
limits: The 45% threshold is fitted on these models and tasks. Voting helps one-shot tasks, not agentic ones.
agent_relevance: Teams are for weak baselines. A strong single-agent loop should not be split into a team.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems - where teams win
finding: Decentralized teams helped on parallel search of a large space; all multi-agent variants hurt on sequential planning.
numbers: Dynamic web navigation: decentralized +9.2%. PlanCraft: -70% to -39% for all multi-agent variants. Finance-Agent: +57% to +80.8%.
limits: Single benchmark per task type.
agent_relevance: Parallel exploration is the one place to spend more agents.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: A taxonomy of 14 failure modes in LLM teams, built from 150 traces, then applied to 1,600+ traces over 7 frameworks. Most failures come from team design, not the base model.
numbers: Three categories: system design 44.2%, inter-agent misalignment 32.3%, task verification 23.5%. Kappa = 0.88. Top modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination 12.4%, disobey task spec 11.8%, incorrect verification 9.1%.
limits: Shares are from specific frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2 and others), labelled partly by an LLM.
agent_relevance: The coordination losses that limit big human teams appear in LLM teams. Gives a checklist for code-side checks.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST) - interventions
finding: Simple team-design fixes help but do not remove failures.
numbers: ChatDev with GPT-4o on ProgramDev: +9.4% success from better role specifications alone; +15.6% from workflow changes.
limits: Case studies on two systems (AG2, ChatDev); gains small.
agent_relevance: An explicit verification step in code is the cheapest team-style gain.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Exploring Collaboration Mechanisms for LLM Agents: A Social Psychology View
finding: Four societies of LLM agents with traits (easy-going or overconfident) and thinking patterns (debate or reflection) tested on MMLU, MATH and chess move validity. Agents show conformity and consensus-seeking like human groups.
numbers: Eight 3-round strategies. MMLU accuracy ranged roughly 34% to 70% by society and strategy; best strategies start with debate. Token cost varied about 2.2x across strategies (4364 vs 1976 average). Three rounds judged efficient; 3 to 10 rounds changed accuracy little.
limits: Mainly ChatGPT (gpt-3.5); effect depends on task; chess differences small.
agent_relevance: Conformity is a failure source in teams of one model; matches G4.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Exploring Collaboration Mechanisms for LLM Agents: A Social Psychology View - conformity and group size
finding: More agents reach consensus more often. Conformity helps when the agents lean right and hurts when they lean wrong.
numbers: Agent counts 2 to 10 tested; odd counts avoid ties; benefits of conformity shrink as rounds increase.
limits: Effect sizes are in figures, not one number; one main model.
agent_relevance: Agreement is not evidence of truth. Do not use it as a pass signal.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five multi-agent debate methods on 9 benchmarks and 4 models mostly fail to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, despite far more compute.
numbers: 36 configs, ANOVA at 0.05: SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; MP never. On Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU only AgentVerse beat CoT (+0.85%); others lost by at least 3.60%. Self-consistency usually beat CoT and debate.
limits: Default settings; debate did better on maths than on coding.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of 'many heads are better' for LLMs. Counts against debate teams in our loop.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate - heterogeneity
finding: Mixing two different models in the debate improved all debate methods, like a diverse human team.
numbers: Heter-SoM beat SoM-average by 6.4%; Heter-EoT beat EoT-average by 8.2%; all heterogeneous MAD beat CoT-average by up to 5.8%.
limits: Only two candidate models; gains are against averages of separate runs.
agent_relevance: Diversity gains come from different models, not different personas of one model.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents
finding: Sampling the single best model many times (Self-MoA) beat mixing different LLMs in many cases. Mixing lowered average quality.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6% over MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0; +3.8% average over MMLU, CRUX, MATH; over 200 experiments using the Vendi diversity score.
limits: Mixing helps only when the models are of similar quality.
agent_relevance: Qualifies c12: team diversity helps only if members are not weaker. Quality first.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) MultiAgentBench (MARBLE)
finding: Benchmark of LLM teams with milestone scores. Graph coordination was best in the research scenario; cognitive planning raised milestone rate 3%.
numbers: Agent count test 1, 3, 5, 7 in a research scenario built from 20 papers with at least 7 authors: overall KPI fell as agents rose; coordination score rose clearly from 1 to 3 agents, task score rose slowly. gpt-4o-mini had the top average task score.
limits: Seven-author papers are a design choice, not a replication of human team studies; numbers read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Fits the human result that a small team is the useful size.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
finding: Uses information-theoretic synergy from human collective-intelligence work to test whether LLM groups act as one unit. Persona plus a 'think about what others might do' prompt gave complementary roles; plain groups did not.
numbers: Preliminary grid: 13 group sizes x 11 temperatures x 50 groups = 7,150 runs (GPT-4.1). Each extra member cut odds of success about 8% (OR 0.92, p<1e-16); temperature +1 raised odds about 50% (OR 1.50). Main runs N=10; also Llama-3.1-8B and 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3.
limits: A simple guessing game with no direct communication; not a science task.
agent_relevance: A direct measure of complementarity (the super-tie idea) and proof prompts can steer it; size hurts.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models - prompt effects
finding: Three randomized conditions: plain, persona, persona plus theory-of-mind prompt. Only the third gave identity-linked differentiation and goal-directed complementarity.
numbers: Results robust across emergence measures and entropy estimators; control groups had strong temporal synergy but little cross-agent alignment.
limits: Effect sizes are in figures; one game.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt line can move a team from aggregate to collective, but only with roles.

source: Chen et al. (2023) AgentVerse
finding: A recruited group of expert agents beat a single chain-of-thought agent on most tasks, but with GPT-3.5 the group sometimes lost to a solo agent because wrong feedback spread.
numbers: Table 1 (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4): FED 81.6 CoT, 81.1 Solo, 85.1 Group / 95.4, 95.8, 96.8; MGSM 80.4, 82.4, 80.8 / 95.2, 96.0, 95.2; Logic Grid (GPT-4) 59.5, 64.0, 66.5. Volunteer, conformity and destructive behaviours observed.
limits: Gains often under 3 points; CoT baseline weak by later standards.
agent_relevance: Team gains are small and model-dependent; weak members add noise.

source: Chen et al. (2023) AgentVerse - horizontal vs vertical
finding: Two team structures: horizontal (democratic) and vertical (one solver, reviewers refine). Vertical suits maths and software, where one refined answer is needed.
numbers: No single figure; design statement with task-wise tests.
limits: Qualitative guidance.
agent_relevance: Solver-plus-reviewer fits our schema better than open debate.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: A single pipeline agent writes whole papers for under $15 each. Its automated reviewer is near human, but the papers have flaws.
numbers: Reviewer F1 0.57 vs humans 0.49; AUC 0.65 for both; at threshold 6 (weak accept); reviews cost $0.25 to $0.50. Failures: hallucinated plot, missing related-work section, ideas leaking future tokens to lower perplexity.
limits: Three ML subfields only; reviewer calibrated on one set.
agent_relevance: Role stages replace a team in code; the reviewer/check step is the weak point.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
finding: A multi-agent system (generate, reflect, rank, evolve with tournaments) improves hypotheses as compute grows. Experts preferred it over other models.
numbers: 203 research goals in ten time buckets showed rising max and top-10 Elo; expert preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64, impact 3.09 of 5 on 15 goals; AML drug repurposing validated in vitro.
limits: Elo is self-judged; expert scores subjective; small expert set.
agent_relevance: A role-split team with a tournament selector; ranking in code fits G5 but risks self-judge bias.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2025) Agent Laboratory
finding: Agent pipeline (literature, experiments, report) with optional human co-pilot checkpoints. Human feedback at each stage raised quality; cost fell 84% vs earlier autonomous methods.
numbers: o1-preview report quality 3.4/5, usefulness 4.4/5; gpt-4o experiments 2.6/5, report 3.0/5, usefulness 4.0/5; o1-mini experiments 3.2/5.
limits: Small researcher survey; ratings subjective.
agent_relevance: Human check points between stages beat full autonomy.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2025) Agent Laboratory - co-pilot vs autonomous
finding: Human co-pilot checkpoints raised self-evaluated scores a little, mostly in clarity and presentation, but lowered significance and contribution. Still below accepted-paper level.
numbers: Autonomous 3.8/10 vs co-pilot 4.13/10 (+0.33); clarity +0.48, soundness +0.35, presentation +0.33, quality +0.13; significance -0.3, contribution -0.1. Co-pilot average 4.38 vs 5.85 for an accepted NeurIPS 2024 paper (-1.45).
limits: Scores come from an LLM self-evaluation and a small human survey.
agent_relevance: Humans in the team polish the paper; they do not fix weak science. Gains are real but small.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist - Elo vs ground truth
finding: The self-judged Elo score tracks accuracy on GPQA diamond questions, which gives some outside check on the tournament selector.
numbers: Top-rated Co-Scientist answer per question reached top-1 accuracy 78.4%; accuracy rose with Elo bucket (50-point buckets) against a 32-sample Gemini 2.0 reference per question.
limits: Elo is auto-evaluated, not ground truth; GPQA is multiple choice, not open hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a ranking tournament can be calibrated against known answers (supports G3 and G5 if checked).

source: Gap note (not a source)
finding: No study found in this run directly tests the 17%-per-decade team growth or complementary super-ties on LLM agents. LLM studies test team size, topology and diversity instead.
numbers: Search APIs were rate-limited and the WebSearch budget was spent; coverage is incomplete.
limits: Virtual Lab (Swanson et al. 2025) and Hao et al. on AI tools and science's focus were not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only; the LLM lesson is that team size costs unless verification exists.

source: Cross-link note (not a source)
finding: c15 (Riedl) and c07 (MAST) bridge to the parallel subfields Coordination and common ground, and Collective intelligence factor c; not covered here.
numbers: n/a
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: n/a
